title: Timure, Nepal: looking back at the 26 August landslide
place: About 7.5 x 8.6 km window of the Bhote Koshi / Trishuli valley at Timure, Rasuwa District, Nepal, near the Gyirong border crossing
mechanism: Candidate explanation: debris, mud and changed river channels alter surface roughness and moisture, which changes radar brightness. Steep slopes also cause radar shadow and layover, which were not screened here.
what_happened: On 26 August 2026 at 02:52 UTC a high-mountain ice-rock avalanche in Nepal sent a debris flow down the valley; seismometers recorded it (USGS). Copernicus Emergency Management Service (EMSR927) mapped the affected area at Timure from imagery of 27 August. The source is far upstream of this window; this view covers the downstream valley where impacts were mapped.

sources.label: UNESCO IHP-WINS: damage grading, Syapru Besi and Timure, 27 August 2026

use_for: Looking back at what a 12-day radar record captured in an affected valley, beside an independent damage map.
Showing where the record has gaps and what questions it cannot answer.
A starting point for future work on whether slower changes before such events can be seen in a long radar record. This page does not show that.
not_for: Not a warning, a forecast, or evidence that losses could have been prevented.
Not a damage map or a measurement of ground movement, speed or stress.
limits: There is no quiet 12-day reference just before the event: 7 August is missing.
The 12 days after the event are not a stable control; clean-up, water and deposits keep changing.
The EMS map and the radar passes are days apart. Mountain shadow and layover were not screened.
Edge cells mix inside and outside. Neighbouring cells are not independent. No accuracy score.
product: NISAR L2 GCOV, L-band, Frequency A, HHHH and HVHV. 10 m linear power averaged over 5 x 5 pixels (50 m), then converted to dB
interval_labels: 19 Aug to 31 Aug, across the event
radar_summary: Inside the EMS-mapped impact area, 497 of 509 cells (50 m) have radar data on all three dates. In HV, 15.7% of them changed by more than 3 dB across the event (19 to 31 Aug), mostly darker, against 1.2% over the next 12 days. 43% changed by less than 1 dB across the event. Click a cell for its values.
tour: The Timure valley in Nepal. Left: radar on 19 August, before the 26 August avalanche. Right: 31 August, after. The red outline is the impact Copernicus EMS mapped.
Left of the line: change across the event. Right: the next 12 days. Same colour scale. Blue is darker, red is brighter.
This is HV. Inside the mapped impact, 15.7% of cells changed by more than 3 dB in HV across the event and 1.2% over the next 12 days, but many hardly changed.
The panel compares the radar with the Copernicus damage map, and lists the ground-movement checks we ran under More detail.
Click a cell to see its values, or press Play to step through all ten dates.
series_note: Ten radar dates, every NISAR pass available here since the data began: 20 Jun, 2 Jul, 14 Jul, 26 Jul, 19 Aug, 31 Aug, 12 Sep, 24 Sep, 6 Oct and 18 Oct 2026 (UTC). 7 August is missing, so 26 Jul to 19 Aug is a 24-day gap. Press Play to step through them. Lines join observations only.
task: After a disaster, an analyst wants to see what the radar recorded in the affected valley, next to the official damage map.
optical_text: The independent evidence here is the Copernicus EMS map, drawn by photo-interpretation of 27 August imagery: the outline of the mapped landslide impact and deposits (red) and the area that was mapped (dashed). It is not a source failure outline. The radar window covers the whole mapped impact.
agreement: Yes, in part. Inside the mapped impact, strong change affected 15.7% of cells across the event against 1.2% over the next 12 days, consistent with a sudden change of the surface. Other cells changed little, so the radar points to where to look rather than drawing the damage outline.

independent_evidence.question: Is there independent evidence of the event?
independent_evidence.text: Copernicus EMS mapped the impact from 27 August imagery; USGS recorded the seismic signal.

reference_extent.question: Can the radar show ground movement before the event?
reference_extent.text: No. The available interferometric data at the source failed quality checks or did not cover it.
